applicability: any non-negative integer: n is divisible by 3 iff the sum of its base-10 digits is divisible by 3

sampling.presentation_filter_rationale: The rule works on any non-negative integer; the range 100–999 is a rendering choice so the digit-sum step has three digits to add (a one-digit example is trivial, a five-digit example overflows the card). The filter pins the digit count and constrains nothing about divisibility.

universality.claim: the digit-sum test is exact: for every non-negative integer n, 3 | n iff 3 | digitsum10(n)
universality.mapping: With b = 10, the whitelisted theorem gives n ≡ digitsum10(n) (mod 9). Since 3 divides 9, reducing mod 3 preserves the congruence: n ≡ digitsum10(n) (mod 3), so 3 | n iff 3 | digitsum10(n).

nulls.reason: digit-sum divisibility test for 3 has no counter-example. The rule is universal for non-negative integers by base-b-digit-sum-congruence with b = 10, reduced modulo 3 (a divisor of b − 1 = 9). Verifier is expected to confirm exhaustively over a stated finite domain.
